summary: Water-cycle vocabulary for ages 7–9: teach the terms evaporation, condensation, precipitation, collection/runoff, transpiration, water vapour and groundwater by pinning each to WHERE it happens and, for the terms that involve one (evaporation, condensation, transpiration), WHAT change of state is occurring. Precipitation, collection/runoff and groundwater describe water moving or being stored, not a change of state. The terms are arranged on a cyclic diagram so the correct sequence can be seen. The core teaching move is placing the easily confused pair evaporation and condensation on opposite arrows of the same loop (the same state change, in opposite directions). Every term is paired with a concrete everyday observation, and the cycle is stressed as a continuous loop with no start or end, driven by the Sun's energy.
misconceptions: Swapping 'evaporation' and 'condensation' — confusing the two opposite directions of state change.
'Clouds are made of water vapour' — clouds are condensed tiny liquid droplets, not invisible vapour.
'The water cycle has a start and an end' — not seeing it as a continuous loop.
'Evaporated water disappears / is used up' — not realising it becomes invisible water vapour still present in the air.
'Precipitation only means rain' — forgetting snow, hail and sleet are precipitation too.
'Rain comes from clouds getting heavy with vapour' — missing that droplets must condense and coalesce first.

activities.title: Label and explore a cyclic water-cycle landscape
steps: Study a labelled cyclic diagram of a landscape: Sun, a lake or puddle, upward arrows showing invisible water vapour rising, a cloud, falling rain, a river, trees, and hidden groundwater below the surface, with arrows forming a ring.
Point to (or on screen, tap) the sun-warmed lake and read/say: 'evaporation — liquid water turns into invisible water vapour, and it happens faster when it is warmer.'
Point to the cloud and read/say: 'condensation — water vapour cools and turns back into tiny liquid droplets that make the cloud.'
Point to the falling rain and say: 'precipitation — water falling as rain, snow, hail or sleet.'
Point to the trees/plants and name 'transpiration' — plants draw up liquid water and release it from their leaves as water vapour (a liquid-to-vapour change, like evaporation but from the plant).

Point to the river and underground layer and name 'collection / runoff' (water gathering and flowing downhill) and 'groundwater' (water that has soaked into the ground and is stored in soil and rock underground).
Trace the ring all the way round, noticing it has no beginning and no end, and that the Sun is the energy that drives it.
activities.insight: Each water-cycle term names something that happens to water at a specific place: a change of state (evaporation, condensation, transpiration), or water falling, flowing or being stored (precipitation, runoff/collection, groundwater). The stages form a continuous loop driven by the Sun, so 'in the correct sequence' is something you can see in the ring itself.

activities.title: Match each term to an everyday observation
steps: Match word cards to picture/phenomenon cards: 'evaporation' ↔ a puddle drying up in the sunshine (or wet washing drying on a line); 'condensation' ↔ droplets forming on a cold glass or misted window; 'precipitation' ↔ rain, snow and hail falling.
Say aloud why each pairing fits, naming the state change (e.g. 'the puddle water turns to vapour, so that's evaporation').
Sort pictures of rain, snow, hail and sleet together under 'precipitation' to see it means more than just rain.
activities.insight: Each technical word describes something children can actually observe, and precipitation covers snow, hail and sleet, not only rain.

activities.title: Sequence the stages and complete the cycle in words
steps: Order a set of stage strips into the cycle: evaporation → condensation → precipitation → collection/runoff, then note the loop returns to evaporation.
Complete a short cloze paragraph describing a water-cycle journey by writing the correct term in each blank.

Match each term to its definition, and choose the correct word to distinguish evaporation from condensation in a described situation ('water vapour cools high up and forms tiny droplets' → condensation).
activities.insight: Correct use of the vocabulary means placing each term in its right slot within a real journey, not just reciting a definition.

activities.title: Boiling-kettle and cold-plate demonstration
steps: Watch (with adult supervision) water being heated in a kettle. Name the change as evaporation: hot liquid water quickly turns into invisible water vapour (in a boiling kettle this happens very fast, and is called boiling). Notice that the white cloud a little way from the spout is not vapour: the vapour has already cooled and condensed into tiny droplets.
Watch while the adult holds a cold plate or lid in the rising steam, keeping your hands well away, and see droplets form on it. Name this as condensation: vapour cooling back into liquid.
Say both words in a sentence describing what just happened, pointing out they are opposite directions of the same change.
activities.insight: Evaporation and condensation are two opposite directions of one state change. In a single demonstration you can see the results of both within a few seconds: the water level slowly drops as liquid turns into invisible vapour, and liquid droplets appear where the vapour cools.

activities.title: Tell the story of a raindrop's journey (spoken production)
steps: Narrate aloud the journey of water starting from a puddle in the Sun, following it all the way until it could fall as rain again.

Use the proper words in sequence: the Sun heats the puddle so water evaporates into water vapour; the vapour rises, cools and condenses into cloud droplets; the droplets join together and grow heavy enough to fall as precipitation (rain, snow or hail); the water collects and runs off into rivers, or soaks into the ground as groundwater, and the cycle repeats.

Respond to follow-up prompts, for example: 'You said the water went up — what is the proper word for water turning into a gas and rising?'; 'When the cloud droplets form, is that evaporation or condensation? Use the word in a sentence.'; 'Where does groundwater fit in your story?'; 'If rain lands on a hill and flows downhill into a river, what do we call that?'
activities.insight: Genuine command of the vocabulary shows up when each term is used correctly in its right slot within a self-produced narrative, not when definitions are recited in isolation.

checkQuestion: Tell me the story of a raindrop's journey around the water cycle — start with a puddle in the Sun and follow the water all the way until it could fall as rain again. Use the proper words as you go, and I'll listen for how you use them.
checkAnswer: The child narrates the cycle using the terms correctly and in sequence: the Sun heats the puddle so the water evaporates into water vapour; the vapour rises, cools and condenses into cloud droplets (condensation); the droplets fall as precipitation (rain, snow or hail); the water collects and runs off (runoff, collection) into rivers and groundwater, and the cycle repeats.
